Concluding Comments
The claim that redundant information should leave a rational belief unaﬀected appears
intuitive and innocuous, and it follows directly from the law of total probability. This law
of total probability, however, implicitly assumes that beliefs are updated using Bayes’ rule.
This provides yet another demonstration of why the rational updating of beliefs depends
on the application of Bayes’ rule. We are currently not aware of this argument having been
made before.
There are two caveats of our uniqueness result: the ﬁrst is that it only shows unique-
ness of Bayes’ rule almost surely. There exist updating rules that satisfy all our assumptions,
but do diﬀer from Bayes’ rule on a set with probability 0. The second is that Bayes’ rule
itself is used in one of the assumptions, Equation (3). This is not circular: we showed that,
supposing that our beliefs are updated by Bayes’ rule, there is no alternative set of beliefs
that satisﬁes the principle of redundant reﬂection. The principle of redundant reﬂection
implies the involvement of Bayes’ rule in this sense.
One advantage of our result is its generality: while we focused on discrete datasets for
the sake of brevity and illustration, all of the steps can be retraced by replacing sums with
integrals. This oﬀers a diﬀerent perspective on probability density functions and improper
priors, concepts to which these kinds of proofs sometimes do not apply. In addition, we
showed in Theorem 1 that any updating rule is uniquely speciﬁed by its behaviour on event
sets ξ and the principle of redundant reﬂection. The theorem thus also applies to updating
rules diﬀering from Bayes’ rule, such as those deﬁned in Fong et al. (2024).
